name: Jamal Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the roof-bolting crew at Slate Hollow mine and operate the bolter on awkward ground. My two-year technical diploma gave me the basics, but I learned the roof by listening to the drill. My partner and I have grown children, and we help our son keep his small repair shop open. That has left less than a month of expenses saved, though I am one of the best operators here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that if AI only sorts forms, the bolter still needs a careful driver. I use an AI app now and then for equipment notices after the fitter checks them. I would still tap the roof and mark every loose patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be glad the machine work stayed, but our savings are thin and my pay is low for a crew lead. One missed week would mean our son got no help with his shop rent. There are few similar mine jobs close by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the bolter shifts and the roof check before each run. I would ask our son what part of his shop costs we could safely stop covering this month. I would not buy new gear on the strength of a quiet AI year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, even with the roof work steady. A calm headline does not make a thin bank account thick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What support could you stop giving your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could cover less of his shop rent for a month, but he would have to agree on a plan. I would not spring it on him at closing time. The mine wage comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the app miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A notice can say a roof bolt was checked without showing whether the rock around it moved. I look at the mark on the wall. The AI notice app cannot hear a loose roof through my boots.

say: I would keep **roof checks** with the bolting crew while AI sorts forms.
I would protect **mine wages** before promising more support for our son’s shop.
think: My **senior skill** cannot cover a missed week with less than a month saved.
Few **nearby mines** make replacing lower-than-usual pay difficult.
do: **Keep** operating the Slate Hollow bolter and checking the roof before each run.
**Discuss** reducing help with our son’s shop rent this month.
feel: **Anxious** about bills despite steady roof work.
S0.quote: The AI notice app cannot hear a loose roof through my boots.
fieldNote: His **technical skill** gives him confidence underground, but his household cushion is thin.
His **traditional family support** has drawn on savings, and he will discuss limits with his son.
He uses AI **occasionally** for notices; continued use is not a new learning action.

steps.text: Keep operating Slate Hollow bolter on scheduled shifts
Discuss reducing help with son’s shop rent this month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can use AI for buying and plans, but a bolting crew still has to test the roof. I would ask the foreman to keep an apprentice beside me when any new schedule starts. A faster form should not erase the learning shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own place may last while robots spread slowly, but the mine might cut a second bolter shift. My lead title will not make up a lost bolter shift’s pay. I could be asked to cover more roof with one less pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI work-order screen from a fitter after the first month of use. I would write down how long bolting and teaching actually take over four weeks. If the foreman cut the apprentice shift, I would ask him to restore it before taking on extra ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I am willing to learn a proven screen, but I cannot make a dangerous roof safe by skipping the apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the foreman?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the time book and the roof marks, then ask where the lost checking minutes went. I would want a straight answer rather than a lecture about efficiency. I have earned that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave if the shift was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are few mines nearby, and I would not walk away from a wage in anger. I would ask the foreman again after a week and look elsewhere only if my own hours actually fell. My partner would need to see the numbers.

say: I would keep an **apprentice shift** beside the bolter when AI changes work orders.
I would ask the **foreman** to explain any lost roof-checking time.
think: My **lead title** may survive while a second bolter shift and its pay disappear.
One less **pair of hands** could make roof work less safe.
do: **Learn** the AI work-order screen from a fitter after its first month.
**Record** four weeks of bolting and teaching time and ask the foreman to restore any cut apprentice shift.
feel: **Anxious** about pay and roof safety under a tighter schedule.
S1.quote: My lead title will not make up a lost bolter shift’s pay.
fieldNote: He expects **office work** to change before hands-on bolting.
His answer centres on **apprenticeship** and the lost wage, not general opposition to AI.
He will learn a **proven screen** after someone else uses it first.

steps.text: Learn AI work-order screen after fitter uses it one month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 changes plans first, while capable bolting robots come around 2031. The mine might buy them, so apprentices need a paid route into machine repair. I would ask the foreman for the purchase plan in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty in 2028 and sixty-three when capable robots arrive. If the mine bought a robot bolter, I might lose the wage before I could retire. We have less than a month saved and our son’s shop cannot carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop paying for the planned family trip this year and talk with our son about the shop help we can afford. I would keep bolting after 2028 while human crews still work. I would take paid mechanical training if the mine posted a real repair job and kept my wages through class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would be awake looking at the roof of our own house and wondering which bill could wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for public help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the wage stopped, I would ask what we qualified for, but I would first seek a paid repair place. I have worked all my life and want a job I can do. Public help would be a bridge, not a plan to sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell him we may have to stop covering shop rent if my mine job goes. He is grown and could look at another space. I would not make a promise that costs us the heating money.

say: I would explain **2028 thinking AI** comes before capable bolting robots around 2031.
I would ask for **paid repair training** and a written purchase plan.
think: At **sixty-three**, a robot bolter could remove the wage before affordable retirement.
Our **tiny savings** and son’s uncertain shop cannot support us for long.
do: **Stop** paying toward the planned family trip this year.
**Discuss** shop-rent support with our son before mine income changes.
**Take** paid mechanical training if a repair job is posted and wages continue.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing mine wages before he can retire.
S2.quote: Public help would be a bridge, not a plan to sit still.
fieldNote: He correctly puts **thinking AI** in 2028 and capable bolting robots around 2031.
Traditional views appear in his preference for a **paid trade** and temporary support if wages stop.
Training requires a **posted repair job**, paid class and continued wages.

steps.text: Stop paying for planned family trip this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and roughly eight to capable roof-bolting robots gives time for a real apprenticeship plan. The mine should train people on repair work while they still earn. I would speak to the foreman about places, not brochures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three when planning AI arrives in 2031 and about sixty-six when capable robots appear in 2034. I might be close to retirement then, but the pension and our thin savings worry me. Repair work could keep money coming if the mine actually needed people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in a paid bolter-repair course next year if the mine posted a job and kept my wages during training. I would request a pension statement and compare monthly income with our bills. I would keep teaching the apprentice while human bolters run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to make a second trade useful. Eight years is enough to test a repair job before betting the household on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of repair would you know already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how a worn feed rail sounds, and I can show where bolts bend under pressure. I would still need instruction on the electronics. A second trade should build on the mine years I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no repair job appears, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my bolter wage and look at the pension again next year. Few other mines are close enough to help. I would not pay for a course just to collect a certificate.

say: I would ask for **paid repair places** before capable bolting robots around 2034.
I would keep **apprenticeships** running while crews still earn.
think: At about **sixty-six**, retirement may be near but the household money may not support it.
A real **repair job** could carry wages longer if the mine needs people.

**Compare** a pension statement with monthly bills.
**Keep** teaching the apprentice during human bolting shifts.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to test a repair route over more years.
S3.quote: A second trade should build on the mine years I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade to thinking AI and about thirteen years to capable bolting robots gives the mine time to keep good apprenticeships alive. I would ask for a plain equipment schedule. Families need to know whether the wages last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and about seventy-one when robots become capable in 2039. I hope to retire before that, but I cannot say so with less than one month saved. The pension statement and our bills will decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the bolting crew and teaching roof checks. I would ask the pension office for a forecast this year and review it with my partner. I would also ask our son for a clear plan to cover his own shop rent by the following year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about retirement money, though the robot date feels far away. Another decade of wages would help us only if the shifts stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your son cannot cover the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would have to decide what part, if any, we could keep paying. I would not empty the heating account for my son’s repair shop. My partner and I would tell him together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop training apprentices near retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, somebody taught me the roof when I was new. The apprentice still needs to know what a loose patch sounds like. I would spend the time while the mine pays us to work.

say: I would ask for a **plain equipment schedule** across the long warning.
I would keep teaching **roof checks** to apprentices while people still run bolters.
think: At about **seventy-one**, I hope to be retired before capable robots arrive but cannot assume it.
Today’s **thin savings** make continued shifts and pension figures essential.
do: **Keep** leading bolting shifts and teaching roof checks.
**Request** a pension forecast and review it with my partner.
**Ask** our son to plan for his own shop rent by next year.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement money despite distant robots.
S4.quote: I would not empty the heating account for my son’s repair shop.
fieldNote: The **2039 robot date** may come after retirement, but retirement funding remains uncertain.

Keeping apprenticeships alive fits his **work-first outlook** and senior skill.

steps.text: Keep leading Slate Hollow bolter shifts while available

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable bolting robots could arrive around 2031 before we have money to retire. A posted repair job with paid instruction would help. I would also need a clear plan for our son’s shop rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches the new bolter crew how roof rock sounds. A robot bolter can put a bolt in the ground, but somebody must decide where the danger begins. My apprentice needs that lesson while there is still a crew to teach it.

headlineQuote: A robot bolter can put a bolt in the ground, but somebody must decide where the danger begins.
portrait: Jamal Quinn is a **58-year-old** roof-bolting crew lead at Slate Hollow mine, with a technical diploma and grown children.
He is highly skilled yet earns **lower pay** and has less than a month saved after helping his son’s shop.
He tries **proven AI tools** occasionally and values hands-on apprenticeship and paid work over promises.
Fast capable robots leave him **alarmed** about wages; a longer warning helps only with real repair jobs and pension figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable bolting robots could arrive around 2031 before affordable retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted repair job** with paid instruction and a plan for his son’s shop rent would help.
